moments.title: Academie francaise founded
moments.body:
Richelieu gives letters patent on 29 January 1635 to formalise an academy that will regulate the French language.

The Academie has 40 'immortels'.
moments.takeaway: Language policy was instituted as a state project under absolutism.

moments.title: First Dictionnaire de l'Academie
moments.body: The first edition appears after sixty years of work. Successive editions follow into the 20th century; the ninth edition was completed in 2024.
moments.takeaway: Codification of standard French is a multi-century institutional process.

moments.title: Gregoire's report on patois
moments.body: Gregoire reports that fewer than half of French citizens speak standard French. The Revolution begins linking language standardisation to national identity.
moments.takeaway: Revolutionary politics turned linguistic uniformity into a republican project.

now.title: French today
now.body: OIF estimates around 320 million French speakers worldwide, with sharply rising figures projected for francophone Africa. Loi Toubon (1994) regulates language in commercial and official contexts.
now.open_questions: How will French evolve as its demographic centre shifts? How will the Academie respond to inclusive writing and other reforms?

items.reflection: French illustrates how strongly state institutions can shape the trajectory of a language over centuries.

moments.title: L'Etre et le Neant
moments.body: Sartre's existentialist treatise appears under Occupation. Phenomenology meets the wartime question of choice under constraint.
moments.takeaway: Foundational French philosophy of the 20th century was written under extreme political conditions.

moments.title: Le Deuxieme Sexe
moments.body: Beauvoir's two-volume study introduces the line 'On ne nait pas femme: on le devient', shaping later feminist theory.
moments.takeaway: The 20th century's leading French intellectuals worked across philosophy, fiction and politics.

moments.title: Camus wins the Nobel
moments.body: Camus, the second-youngest Nobel literature laureate at the time, dies in a car accident in 1960.
moments.takeaway: International recognition placed French literature at the centre of post-war cultural debate.

now.title: French letters today
now.body: Contemporary writing includes prizewinning authors with diverse backgrounds (Modiano, Erpenbeck, NDiaye, Bouraoui). Translation flows have shifted with global publishing.
now.open_questions: How are postcolonial francophone literatures reshaping the French canon?

items.reflection: Major French intellectual movements have repeatedly emerged in dialogue with political crisis.

moments.title: Parlez-vous franglais?
moments.body:
Etiemble's polemic against anglicisms popularises 'franglais' as a term of criticism.

Debate over English borrowing intensifies.
moments.takeaway: Language anxieties have recurred in similar forms across the 20th century.

moments.title: Loi Toubon
moments.body:
French law mandates French in commercial advertising, employment contracts and public-sector communication.

The Constitutional Council narrows some provisions on freedom-of-expression grounds.
moments.takeaway: Language regulation works alongside, not in place of, constitutional rights.

moments.title: Academie endorses 'courriel'
moments.body:
Following Quebec's lead, the Academie recommends 'courriel' for email.

Later recommendations include 'mot-diese' for hashtag and 'jeu video en nuage' for cloud gaming.
moments.takeaway: Official terminology and everyday usage often diverge in practice.

now.title: Linguistic policy today
now.body: Inclusive writing debates, regional language rights and digital terminology continue. Le Robert and Larousse track usage rather than prescribe it.
now.open_questions: How will France balance the Academie's recommendations against international French usage?

items.reflection: Cycles of borrowing and resistance are themselves part of French linguistic history.

moments.title: Onesime Reclus coins 'francophonie'
moments.body: The geographer Reclus introduces the term to describe the community of French speakers worldwide.
moments.takeaway: The concept of a francophone community predates institutional structures.

moments.title: ACCT founded
moments.body: The Agence de cooperation culturelle et technique (later OIF) is founded as the institutional core of la Francophonie.
moments.takeaway: International francophone institutions emerged with decolonisation.

moments.title: African demographic centre
moments.body:
Projections suggest the majority of French speakers will live in Africa by 2050.

DR Congo and other states with French as official or working language drive the shift.
moments.takeaway: The geography of major world languages is being reshaped by African demography.

now.title: Francophonie today
now.body: OIF includes 88 states and governments. Many use French as a second language alongside others; education systems remain central to its spread.
now.open_questions: How does African francophone literature and media reshape the language? What role will French play alongside English and Mandarin globally?

items.reflection: The future of a language often depends on demographic trends well outside the country whose name it bears.
